title: How to Stop Package Theft in an Apartment Building: What Actually Works in Older East Bay Buildings

findings.quote: Cameras record theft; a controlled drop point prevents it.
findings.root_cause: STD-HONEST / EVD-CITATION-REQUIREMENT: the hook converts a reasonable risk-reduction recommendation into an assured outcome and contrasts it with categorical claims that cameras do not prevent theft. The table itself acknowledges deterrence and shared-code risk. Security.org supports layered precautions, not zero theft or the unsourced claim that footage rarely recovers packages. The conclusion/FAQ also overstate low cost without property quotes. No AEBP comparative performance example is documented.
findings.fix:
Replace the Quick Answer opening with: "To reduce package theft in an apartment building, start with where deliveries are left and who can reach them. Cameras can document incidents and may deter theft; controlled access can reduce opportunities to take packages. No option eliminates the risk."
Replace the shared script opening with: "How can you reduce package theft in an apartment building? Start with where deliveries are left and who can reach them. Cameras can document incidents and may deter theft, but they work best alongside a controlled delivery area."
Replace "Doesn't stop the theft, and footage rarely gets a package back" with "Does not physically secure packages; deterrence and recovery are not guaranteed."
Replace the More cameras paragraph with: "Camera footage can help document an incident. Strongly recommended best practice: use cameras alongside controlled access and prompt pickup, rather than relying on footage alone."
Replace "you can make your building a much harder target for very little money" with "you can start by checking existing doors and delivery arrangements before pricing improvements."
Replace FAQ 1's final sentence with: "A written policy and repairs to existing hardware may be lower-cost starting points; a new package room needs a property-specific quote."
Apply the same prevention wording to the excerpt, script on both pages, and GBP/social/SMS lead-ins before distribution.
findings.future_prevention: Review titles, excerpts, FAQs and distribution copy for absolute outcome claims; retain the anecdote log's explicit lack of a proven keypad-versus-camera case.

findings.quote: Confirm every common-area entry door closes, latches and locks on its own (Civil Code §1941.3)
findings.root_cause: GATE-LEGAL-ACCURACY / STD-TRUST-SIGNALS: the citation makes automatic closing/latching a universal statutory duty. Section 1941.3(a)(3) addresses code-compliant locking mechanisms on specified exterior common-area doors; it does not itself impose that blanket closer requirement. The section has scope limits/exceptions, including designated historic buildings, material for an older-building article. The Step One compliance-fix sentence repeats the conflation. Statutory text inspected at https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-civ/division-3/part-4/title-5/chapter-2/section-1941-3/; the official Legislature endpoint returned 403.
findings.fix:
Replace the checklist item with: "Check required common-area entry locks. Strongly recommended best practice: test any existing door closer and confirm the door latches reliably."
Replace the Step One closing paragraph with: "Required by law: for covered multifamily buildings, Civil Code §1941.3(a)(3) addresses locking mechanisms on exterior doors serving common areas with access to dwelling units, subject to the section's scope and exceptions. Strongly recommended best practice: keep existing closers working so doors latch reliably. Before changing doors or converting a closet into package storage, have a qualified professional check applicable fire, egress and accessibility requirements. See our landlord security duties guide for the broader rules."
Retain the statute and security-guide links.
findings.future_prevention: Separate the statutory hardware duty from operational closer recommendations, and review retrofit advice against scope and fire/egress requirements.

findings.quote: No California statute requires a package room or lockers
findings.root_cause: EVD-CITATION-REQUIREMENT: absence of package storage from §1941.3's list supports a statement about that section, not a conclusion about every California statute or every property's requirements. This is an unsupported breadth issue, not evidence that a general locker mandate exists. The same assertion occurs in Quick Answer, Key Facts, conclusion and FAQ 2. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-civ/division-3/part-4/title-5/chapter-2/section-1941-3/.
findings.fix:
Replace the Quick Answer sentence with: "Civil Code §1941.3 does not itself require a package room or lockers; separate property-specific requirements and commitments may still matter."
Replace the Key Facts answer with: "Not under Civil Code §1941.3 itself. That section addresses specified locks, not package storage."
Replace FAQ 2's first two sentences with: "Civil Code §1941.3 does not itself require either. That does not settle every building's obligations: check applicable local requirements, approvals and lease commitments."
Replace the conclusion's opening with: "No setup eliminates every theft, and Civil Code §1941.3 does not itself require a package room."
findings.future_prevention: Narrow negative legal claims to the authority actually checked; do not infer all-law absence from one statutory list.

findings.quote: thieves have used a carrier key to enter a Berkeley apartment building and open its mailboxes.
findings.root_cause: GATE-LOCAL-ACCURACY: the body correctly attributes the master-key theory to the building manager, but the Key Facts row turns it into a confirmed identification. NBC's October 2022 report describes apparent postal-key use and the manager's belief. Verified by direct retrieval after the browser search tool returned 403. https://www.nbcbayarea.com/news/local/east-bay/berkeley-mail-thieves/3027839/
findings.fix: Replace the Postal keys fact cell with: "An Oakland carrier's postal keys were stolen in May 2024. In a separate Berkeley incident reported in October 2022, thieves entered with a key that the building manager believed was a carrier master key." Keep both NBC citations.
findings.future_prevention: Preserve attribution and uncertainty when compressing reporting into tables and answer boxes.

findings.quote: Low (Amazon's install partners describe it as no cost to the property; confirm current terms)
findings.root_cause: GATE-LOCAL-ACCURACY / EVD-CURRENCY-CHECK: ASK4's cited June 26, 2026 article explicitly discusses the UK market. Its no-cost offer does not establish East Bay eligibility or pricing. Attribution and 'confirm current terms' help, but the table still assigns a local cost tier from a different market. This is an evidence gap, not proof Amazon charges US properties. Direct source read: https://www.ask4.com/resources/blog/amazon-key-for-business-smarter-amazon-deliveries-for-your-building . Amazon's own technical explanation supports verified temporary access, not the current local price: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/iot/building-a-virtual-fob-with-amazon-key-for-business-and-aws-iot/
findings.fix:
Replace the carrier-access cost cell with: "Confirm current U.S. property eligibility, installation costs and ongoing fees directly with the provider."
Replace the source-list entry with: "Amazon Key delivery-access mechanism: Amazon's explanation of verified, time-limited building access. Confirm current local availability and terms directly with Amazon." Link to Amazon's own explanation. Keep the cost unquantified unless a current U.S. offer is verified.
findings.future_prevention: Check source country, product variant, date and eligibility before importing vendor prices into local comparisons.
